name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: State Superintendent Jill Underly requests $2.75 billion, new school funding system
description: Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly is proposing that the state spend an additional $2.75 billion on Wisconsin’s schools and make major changes to the education funding formula to take the burden of paying for  schools off local property taxpayers. “It’s time to fix Wisconsin’s school funding formula,” Underly said in a two-minute video posted to […]
text:
“It's time to fix Wisconsin’s school funding formula,” Underly said in a two-minute video posted to social media Friday. Underly speaks to reporters after delivering her sixth State of Education address.  (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly is proposing that the state spend an additional $2.75 billion on Wisconsin’s schools and make major changes to the education funding formula to take the burden of paying for  schools off local property taxpayers.
“It’s time to fix Wisconsin’s school funding formula,” Underly said in a two-minute video posted to social media Friday. “The era of operating referendums needs to come to an end. Our schools shouldn’t have to go back to their communities time and time again, asking property taxpayers for more money because of a broken school funding formula.” 
Wisconsin public schools have relied increasingly on property tax increases sought at the ballot box through referendum requests to meet an array of costs, including staff pay, course offering, electric and water bills.
According to a Wisconsin Policy Forum report published Friday, about 58% of 155 school referendum requests were approved in 2026 — a steep dropoff in approval rates during even-year elections. Typically, there is a higher rate of approvals during presidential and midterm election years, but this was the lowest approval rate in an even-year since 2010. 
The report also notes that a higher proportion of requests are operational rather than building capital requests. In previous years, there’s been about an even divide between the types of requests, but this year, about 80% of requests were for operations. The report concluded that the turn to operational referendums “signals the fiscal stress that some school districts are facing.” 
“It arises from multiple sources, including increased staffing to meet rising student needs, declining student enrollment, and a tight labor market and especially high inflation after the pandemic’s peak,” the report states. “State policy also has played a primary role.” 
Despite school districts’ needs, the approval rate for operational requests, 54%, was lower than the overall rate.
Underly is seeking to shift a larger portion of education costs to the state. 
Democratic state lawmakers and Gov.-elect David Crowley will write and approve the next state budget, but the process of drafting it starts with agencies putting forth their own proposals. 
Underly’s request for the 2027-29 budget includes a slate of changes to the way that schools are funded. 
Under her proposal, school districts would receive a significant increase to their school revenue limits, which cap the amount that districts can bring in through a combination of property taxes and state aid each year. There would be a boost of $1,108 per student in the first year of Underly’s budget and an additional $374 per student in the second year. 
The increases would be in addition to the $325 per student annual increases that school districts received through Gov. Tony Evers’ 400-year budget veto in the 2023 budget. The agency says that the increases are meant to help schools catch up with inflation. Inflationary increases to revenue limits were eliminated in 2009 during the recession, and since then, increases to revenue limits have been based on lawmakers’ appetite to provide them.
Underly’s proposal would once again tie future increases to the rate of inflation. 
The state’s special education reimbursement rate would be raised to 50% in the first year of the DPI  budget proposal and 60% in the second year. 
Another shift Underly proposed is making special education support a “sum sufficient” allocation, meaning that the state would guarantee a set reimbursement rate even if costs changed, as opposed to a “sum certain” allocation, where the state offers is a fixed amount of money that might or might not meet its projected rate of reimbursement, depending on costs.
Wisconsin Public Education Network Executive Director Heather DuBois Bourenane said in a statement that Underly’s proposal “takes a serious step toward addressing the root of the problem with Wisconsin’s unfair and inadequate funding formula.” 
“Wisconsin voters signaled last week that it’s time for Wisconsin to catch up to the rest of the nation and stop playing politics with school budgets while our kids and local taxpayers pay the price,” DuBois Bourenane said. 
Republicans have controlled of the state Legislature since Underly took office in 2021, and  often ignored her budget proposals and declined to invite her to make presentations to the legislative budget committee. 
Underly’s proposal this year could get more serious consideration from Crowley and Democrats who will be leading the budget writing process, but it will be in competition with a variety of other priorities and it’s unclear how much of Underly’s $2.75 billion proposal will make it into the final budget. 
The plan also seeks to help disadvantaged districts by shifting nearly $2 billion to Wisconsin’s equalization aid formula.
The equalization aid formula considers a number of factors including number of students, operational and debt service costs, and local property valuations. 
Equalization aid tends to provide districts with lower property wealth with more aid. Under the plan, districts that could potentially lose aid would be provided with a one-time payment.
The agency is also proposing that the state apply an additional 20% funding weight for economically disadvantaged students and English learners.
The Wisconsin Policy Forum report noted that “the same voter concerns about affordability widely seen as a major factor in sweeping Democrats into power appear to have played a material role in depressing referendum approval rates.”
DPI’s budget presentation asserts that the plan could be implemented without increasing the statewide property tax levy.
Affordability is a top priority for Crowley and incoming Democratic lawmakers. The state will enter 2027 with a $3 billion budget surplus, which could be tapped to address affordability  issues. It’s a much different financial position than in 2009, the last time Democrats had control of the state Senate, Assembly and governor’s office and the state had a $6 billion budget deficit.
Democrats have said that investing in schools could help bring down property taxes. Incoming Assembly Speaker Greta Neubauer has said that they want to stop the cycle of referendum requests to property taxpayers, make changes to the funding formula and provide free schools to help bring down families’ grocery costs.
“I think it’s possible that we will propose some changes in the school funding formula, but our No. 1 priority is to get kids and families the resources that they need,” Neubauer said. 
However, other Democrats, including incoming Senate Majority Leader Dianne Hesselbein, have discussed wanting to study potential changes to education funding and Gov.-elect Crowley has suggested he might appoint a blue ribbon commission to look at taxation.
In her video, Underly said the state does not need to study the issue further. 
“We don’t need to start from scratch. We don’t need another committee. We don’t need more rounds of studies or a series of proposals,” Underly said. “We know what needs to change, and we have the framework to do it. Now, we need state leaders to come together and put the solution into action.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska legislative task force hears overwhelming public support for more investment in schools
description: Alaskans from across the state weighed in on lawmaker proposals to boost K-12 schools during nearly 10 hours of public comment on Thursday. They addressed an initial draft of recommendations from a joint legislative task force on education funding. The task force released its draft report this week where it recommended increasing state education funding […]
text:
School buses park outside the playground of Xóots Elementary School in Sitka on Oct. 6, 2025 (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaskans from across the state weighed in on lawmaker proposals to boost K-12 schools during nearly 10 hours of public comment on Thursday. They addressed an initial draft of recommendations from a joint legislative task force on education funding.
The task force released its draft report this week where it recommended increasing state education funding with inflation, funding school facilities and instruction separately, addressing a massive backlog in maintenance and contracting an adequacy study to evaluate the state’s spending levels.
 
Written public comments to the task force on education funding are due by December 8 and can be emailed to TFEF@akleg.gov or edfundtaskforce@akleg.gov
Over the next two months, the draft report will be further refined, designed, and finalized prior to being officially submitted by the first day of the 2027 legislative session.

Anchorage Democratic Sen. Löki Tobin, co-chair of the task force, opened the all-day hearing by saying the study will alleviate the political battles over state spending per student, known as the base student allocation. 
“We need this information to ensure that we put the right resources into the right components for our school system,” she said. “But we do not have that independent analysis that is absolutely critical to funding our education system.” 
In the meantime, the task force members asked for public input on a state definition for “adequate education.” They also introduced short, mid and long-term recommendations related to school maintenance, the legislative budgeting process, teacher recruitment and retention, transportation and others. Public comment is open until Dec. 8. 
Tobin said that it will be her focus as she was reappointed to chair the Senate Education Committee for the next two years.
Dozens of Alaska parents, students, teachers, principals, superintendents and education advocates testified in person in Anchorage, Fairbanks, Juneau and Kenai — as well as over the phone — urging support for state investment in education.     

Susan Nedza, superintendent of the Hoonah City School District, testifies before the task force on education funding in Juneau on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Susan Nedza, superintendent of the Hoonah City School District in Southeast Alaska, spoke in person in Juneau. 
“If the recommendations in this report reach reality, school staff will be able to focus efforts on our true purpose: students,” she said. “The focus now is on the stress and constant priority of stretching and finding funds to cover the bare basics instead of the well-being of students in our care.”
Many testifiers expressed support for investment in teachers and staff — to reduce vacancies, high turnover and growing class sizes — and much-needed school building repairs. They also pointed to the need for further investment in school nutrition programs, special education services, Alaska Native languages, the Alaska Reads Act, extracurricular opportunities and pathways to careers. 
Some expressed concern that families’ choice to enroll in homeschool programs should be protected, and that the state should not enact any changes to homeschool programs or current standards. 
School officials spoke to skyrocketing costs for heating buildings and keeping facilities operational, and said repairs go years without attention. They expressed support for the task force’s recommendation of a separate funding stream for school facilities costs aside from instructional dollars. 
“Facility funding, rising energy costs and improving conditions for our classrooms, keeping a roof intact or heating the building during the Alaskan winter should never require cutting teachers, class offerings or student support or student activities,” said Jason Weber, superintendent of Valdez City Schools. Many districts across the state have had to make such cuts in recent years. 
Support for education funding bill comes as Alaska districts grapple with ongoing deficits

“Roughly 70% of our school’s budget is related to maintenance,” said Rhonda Pitka, vice president of the Tanana Chiefs Conference and chief of the Village of Beaver in the Yukon Flats. She said they struggle to hire and keep maintenance workers to complete repairs. “This is a critical issue, and it affects the safety and usability of school facilities,” she said. 
Pitka and several officials testified that the rising operational costs also hurt school districts’ ability to offer competitive wages to hire and retain teachers. 
“Overcrowded kindergarten classrooms with high needs — this is tough to have a classroom full of young learners with limited support and lack of teacher aides,” she said. “We face difficulty hiring and retaining teachers in our areas, especially our special education aides, because of the low wages and the benefit issues with the state.”
Grant Guy, principal of Wood River Elementary School in Fairbanks, spoke to how the teacher shortage is burning out teachers in his district. He said that’s particularly acute for special education teachers and paraprofessionals. 
“The amount of time, energy, and cost to train those individuals are immense, and oftentimes by the time they start learning what they need to do to help students de-escalate from situations, they are so burnt out that they go and find positions that pay them more for much less stress,” he said.     

Christine Johnson, a Juneau resident and mother of four, testifies to the task force on education funding on the importance of supporting special education services on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Christine Johnson, a mother of four in Juneau, spoke to the struggle to receive special education support for her child, when the district lacked staff and funding.
“Special education is not an optional program. It is an essential part of providing an adequate public education,” she said. “When a student needs speech therapy, occupational therapy, behavioral support, assistive technology, specialized instruction, or additional support, those needs do not disappear because a district can’t afford the staff or resources to provide them.” 
Many testifiers expressed support for an increase to the state’s per student funding formula and said it would create more stability for districts if the Legislature approved education funding earlier in the year — one of the task force’s top recommendations.
“Make funding stable, timely, and consistent,” said Jason Hlasney, superintendent of the Lower Kuskokwim School District, which serves 22 rural schools across 22,000 miles. He said students need opportunities that foster hope.
“This fall, I asked our students and communities what they hope for. Students asked for welding, carpentry, mechanics, aviation, among other careers. They want to be college and career ready, and they dream of becoming nurses, dentists, hunting guides, and all the various things,” he said. “They ask for more Alaska Native teachers. Our students need learning that connects to real work close to home, from teachers who stay long enough to know every child.”    

Four wheelers and bicycles sit outside the Anna Tobeluk Memorial School on a frosty morning in Nunapitchuk. October 12, 2023. (Photo by Claire Stremple/Alaska Beacon)
 

Nedza, the superintendent in Hoonah, was among those who expressed concern that budget cuts for school nutrition programs are hurting students, and she said they should be part of what is considered adequate funding.
“Some schools have stopped providing meals, provide only some meals, charge students or rely on an increasingly limited general fund to cover this cost,” she said, and added Hoonah’s costs have increased so that the district spends roughly $100,000 on the lunch program each year. 
“Nutritious school meals and universal free meal programs are directly linked to better student attendance, improved focus and higher academic achievement,” she said. “At least nine states already have universal free meals at school, and Alaska needs to follow suit.”
Concerns raised around potential changes to homeschool programs
Several parents, students and advocates testified in support of homeschooling options, called correspondence programs, which vary across the state. Several parents told lawmakers homeschooling is a better fit for their educational and family needs. 
Kendal Kruse, a mother of five in Palmer and a member of the Matanuska-Susitna School Board, gave personal testimony opposing any changes to homeschool policies that she said would force students into neighborhood schools.
“One in five kids is using a correspondence school in Alaska. That is a huge percentage of our student population, for us to be highly concerned about repealing or reducing the access to these programs for students that need them, and I think that’s a huge mistake,” she said.
Kruse and others expressed concern about language in the task force’s draft report recommending districts investigate ways to incorporate homeschool students into neighborhood schools, which cited research that said “in-person learning significantly outperforms online and distance learning.”
Several parents also took issue with the task force recommendation to review statutes to ensure homeschool students are being provided an adequate education, noting that current law allows broad exemptions from “statewide content standards, proficiency assessments, and fiscal audits.” 
But Wasilla elementary school teacher Kathleen Yerbich spoke in favor of state testing for all homeschooled students, as she sees students in her classroom who have fallen behind after years of homeschooling. “This is the part no one talks about,” she said. 
“Some parents readily admit that the job was harder than they anticipated. Their kid didn’t want to do the assignment. They were too busy with sports to do all that was required, and so on. We are placing the parents’ right to choose above educating our children. I believe that all children should be tested yearly to see how they are doing,” Yerbich said. 
“All kids deserve an excellent education. They deserve a chance to learn to the best of their abilities and to be challenged to the next level. The elementary years go by quickly. It is unfair to children for the state of Alaska not to be diligent in making sure they are learning,” she said.
Following the hearing Thursday, task force member and Juneau Democratic Sen. Jesse Kiehl said the task force will likely revise some of the language in the recommendations to address homeschool families’ concerns. 
“We’re looking at opening more opportunities for school districts to offer those families more choices, not fewer,” he said. “And at the same time to make sure that parents have the tools to know if their kids are making progress, and so I think that we can reword that and hopefully put some of those fears to bed.”
Raising the BSA with inflation
School officials and advocates are urging an increase to per student funding next year. They say the BSA should increase  at least $1,011 per student — a roughly 15% bump that would cost the state $254.6 million.     

Lisa Parady, executive director of the Alaska Council of School Administrators, testifies before the legislative task force on education funding in Juneau on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Lisa Parady, executive director of the Alaska Council of School Administrators, testified Thursday that the figure was calculated with the state legislative finance division to account for inflation since 2017. The organization is also calling for investment in school facilities, and to restore a defined-benefit pension system for public service employees, including teachers. 
While the large majority of testifiers urged more state spending on schools, some — like Josh Church of Fairbanks, who recently ran for lieutenant governor as Republican Dave Bronson’s running mate — urged legislators to look at educational requirements and outcomes instead of more state spending. 
“We need to look at, not how do we protect the education system in the state, but how do we produce the best results for the kids of this state. So the answer to this is not always more money, more money,” he said. “The solution for more money, additional pensions, whatever it might be — we’ve been chasing that rabbit for years and years, and more money does not solve a problem if you don’t get to the underlying causes.”
Kiehl said the incoming Legislature will be working with presumptive Gov.-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins on the budget, the task force recommendations and first priorities for funding education. 
Kiehl, who also co-chairs the Senate Finance Committee, said his first priority would be addressing the BSA so that districts have predictable funding. “If we can take that off the table before the rest of the budget process, school boards around the state will have a chance to focus on education policy instead of rewriting the budget eight times,” he said.
Alaska is seeing high state oil revenues due to the surge in oil prices driven by the U.S. war on Iran, and Kiehl said schools are a top priority. 
“The business of the Legislature is the business of “no” and figuring out which things to say no to, and where we have to say yes for Alaska’s future, we’re going to say yes in schools,” he said. “Exactly how much? Exactly when? That’s the hard work that starts in January.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Most school levies failed, which prompts a review of how we fund schools
description: The recent election sent a contradictory message about Minnesota public education. About 73% of voters approved a constitutional amendment increasing payouts from the state’s Permanent School Fund, which generates revenue from school trust lands. It is welcome news, but small: $33 more per student, from about $68 to $101, with the first payment in July […]
text:
The author argues that school districts have become overly reliant on local property taxpayers, who are in turn increasingly rejecting local levies. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)The recent election sent a contradictory message about Minnesota public education. About 73% of voters approved a constitutional amendment increasing payouts from the state’s Permanent School Fund, which generates revenue from school trust lands. It is welcome news, but small: $33 more per student, from about $68 to $101, with the first payment in July 2027. 
Yet voters rejected 55 of the 83 school funding questions on local ballots, according to unofficial results.
How do we reconcile those results? The amendment was promoted as a way to raise school funding without raising taxes. Do Minnesotans support public education when it won’t cost them anything, but pull back when their property taxes are at stake?
If so, students unlucky enough to live in a community that is unable or unwilling to pay more in property taxes will get fewer opportunities than their classmates in other communities. 
Does that seem fair? 
Education is a statewide responsibility 
Voters should have a say in major local spending decisions, and school boards should be accountable for their budgets. The basic opportunities available to students should not be determined primarily by a community’s willingness to repeatedly approve property tax increases. 
If Minnesota truly believes public education is a statewide priority, shouldn’t the responsibility for funding it also be shared statewide?
Rejection of school levies is not new, but the Minnesota School Boards Association reports that just 30% of operating referendums, 36% of bond requests and 42% of capital project requests passed this year. In 2024, 35 of 64 school questions failed. 
The gap shows up in rural Minnesota too. In the Lake Park-Audubon district, the schools’ own leaflet estimated that its two school funding questions together would cost about $60 a year, or $5 a month, on a $300,000 home, with lake cabins paying nothing. Even so, both failed with just over 40% of the vote. In Frazee-Vergas, about 46% supported its request. 
When a levy fails, the financial pressure does not disappear. Last November, Marshall voters rejected a $2 million, 10-year operating referendum. The school board then approved cuts of at least $1.8 million for 2026-27, including districtwide staffing reductions and the elimination of programs. 
In Deer River, after multiple referendums failed, the district must now cut $2 million, or 12% of its budget. Nearly 70% of that budget goes toward staff costs, so most of the cuts will fall on staffing. 
In a June 2026 survey by the Minnesota Rural Education Association, 61% of 105 responding rural districts reported reducing instructional staff, and the survey’s write-up mentions larger class sizes and fewer secondary course offerings. The whole community feels it. If we believe rural communities must remain viable, we must consider what happens when their schools cannot adequately serve their students.
Is it time to rethink how Minnesota pays for schools?
Perhaps the bigger problem is not that voters reject referendums. Rather, Minnesota has become too dependent on local property taxpayers to finance an essential statewide responsibility. 
That creates inequities. Communities with different property tax capacity, enrollment and economic circumstances face very different odds of raising the same amount. A student’s opportunities should not depend so heavily on their ZIP code. 
It is time to examine a different balance between statewide and local funding. Options include a more progressive income tax; a carefully designed tax on accumulated wealth; and redirecting existing alcohol, tobacco and cannabis tax revenue to schools.
Each option shifts who pays, and the state’s own numbers show how differently. The Department of Revenue’s 2026 tax incidence study found that the individual income tax is the only major progressive tax. Redirecting money the state already collects is another option. Alcohol and tobacco taxes together raised about $655 million in fiscal year 2024, compared with $14.9 billion from the income tax, and the cannabis tax is now 15%. Dedicating that revenue to schools would not raise anyone’s taxes, but the general fund would lose it unless lawmakers replaced it. 
A wealth tax is a different kind of idea. This year’s HF 4616, which proposed a 1% tax on wealth above $10 million, would have reached about 5,600 taxpayers and raised an estimated $288 million in its first year, but it never reached a floor vote, and opponents warned of avoidance and departures. Just 4 of the 38 nations in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development countries had net wealth taxes in 2017, down from 12 in 1990, and the OECD found their revenues generally low.  
Another starts with the local tax base itself. Seasonal recreational property, such as lake cabins, is excluded from the base for operating referendums, so other property owners carry that cost. The exclusion dates to 2001. Cabin owners still pay other taxes, including the state levy and local building levies, but whether they should share operating costs deserves a hearing. 
None of these options is a complete solution. Each deserves an honest look at who pays, who benefits and how reliably the revenue can support schools.

description: The need for mental health and other wellness services among Native American students outpaces what’s available with existing funding, according to data collected earlier this year and presented recently to South Dakota educators. text:
Dorothy Aguilera-Black Bear speaks to attendees during a breakout session at the annual Indian Education Summit in Pierre, South Dakota, on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/111226-Building-from-Strengths-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
The need for mental health and other wellness services among Native American students outpaces what’s available with existing funding, according to data collected earlier this year and presented recently to South Dakota educators.
Dorothy Aguilera-Black Bear and Brooke Rumper, of the Central Comprehensive Center, asked South Dakota principals whose schools have at least one Native American student to identify the needs and available resources for those students. Of the 673 asked to participate in the survey, Aguilera-Black Bear and Rumper got responses from 157.
The pair shared their findings Thursday at the annual Indian Education Summit in Pierre. Federal grants helped fund the research, and the project is in partnership with the state Department of Tribal Relations and state Office of Indian Education.
“The capacity for schools to have those consistent needs be supported is really difficult,” said Aguilera-Black Bear.
‘We can do it’: A rural school near two Native American reservations nearly doubles its attendance

They’re bringing their findings to tribal education directors to dig deeper into the data, “because they’re very close to what’s going on in the schools that serve their tribal citizens,” said Aguilera-Black Bear. With the feedback from Thursday’s presentation, her team is hoping to help educators create action plans to address their students’ needs.
Nearly 60% of the survey respondents said their schools don’t have enough funding to provide the mental health and reproductive health education and access that students need. Some respondents also mentioned a lack of student access to community elders and knowledge keepers, and a struggle to hire staff with culturally relevant or trauma-informed training.
The survey also showed that many Native students in South Dakota lack access to secure housing, reliable food sources outside of school, and clothing and hygiene products.
Martina Moves Camp is a transition specialist at Crazy Horse School in Wanblee, on the Pine Ridge Reservation. She said her students experience challenges that are reflected in the data, including struggles with basic needs like food and clothing, but seeing the collaboration of researchers and educators gives her hope for finding solutions.
“We’re meeting that need, but we aren’t where a lot of other schools are,” Moves Camp said. “And I can’t wait for the day for our school to be where we are creating those culture-bearers, where they are able to be teachers to their next generation.”

name: California
title: Tax the rich — sometimes. California voters sent mixed signals with ballot measures
description: California voters shot down a tax on billionaires' assets but said yes to a high-income tax. They were just two of the five tax questions on the ballot.
text:
In summary
California voters shot down a tax on billionaires’ assets but said yes to a high-income tax. They were just two of the five tax questions on the ballot.


California voters faced big questions about money in this election, and the results sent mixed signals about how the electorate feels about taxation.
They want to tax the rich — but only sometimes. They want the money counters at the Franchise Tax Board to stay far away from personal assets, but are leaving the door open for future taxes or taxes on other people.
On Election Day, voters: 

Rejected Proposition 40, an effort to levy a first-of-its-kind wealth tax on billionaires
Rejected Proposition 41, a taxation transparency measure 
Approved Proposition 42, a ban on wealth taxes and retroactive taxes 
Rejected Proposition 43, an attempt to make it more difficult for local governments to raise taxes
Approved Proposition 3, a proposal to make permanent a tax on high-income earners

Voters also approved several high-profile local taxes, including two measures to fund the Bay Area’s regional transit systems, including Muni and BART, and a half-cent sales tax to fund firefighting in the city of Los Angeles.
The mixed outcome, experts say, shows that California voters are embracing tax hikes — but only when they can ensure the money is funding tangible services they support.
“Voters are willing to open up their wallet if they believe it’s for a good cause … and that it’s actually going to that place,” said Brandon Castillo, a prominent ballot measure strategist in California.
It also demonstrates voters’ willingness to support taxes that likely won’t affect their own pocketbook, said Mark Baldassare, survey director of the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California.
“We are a very progressive state where voters, particularly today when affordability weighs on them, have a tendency to say somebody else will be paying taxes, not me.”
Still, that “not me” attitude didn’t stretch as far as the state’s contentious billionaire tax, which faced opposition from business interests, Democrats and deep-pocketed Silicon Valley executives alike.
Why did the billionaire tax fail?
The failure of the billionaire tax represents the most stunning defeat of Election Day for progressive Democrats who tried unsuccessfully to capitalize on souring sentiment toward the ultra-wealthy amid high gas prices and worsening inflation for average Californians. How could the most progressive measure in the most progressive state fail during a “blue wave” election?
“California voters are sometimes more conservative on ballot propositions than they are on voting for candidates,” said Christian Grose, a political science and public policy professor at USC.
In recent years, voters through ballot measures got tougher on crime, shot down a minimum wage increase and rejected efforts to make it easier to pass local bonds. In fact, voters upheld the death penalty the last time it appeared on the ballot even though the state has not executed anyone since 2006. In a historic decision, Gov. Gavin Newsom also earlier this month commuted all death row sentences to life without parole. 
Rob Stutzman, a Republican political consultant, said this trend likely holds true because ballot initiatives — including taxation questions — generally ask voters to consider one issue at a time and are presented in a nonpartisan manner. In contrast, voting for a liberal or conservative candidate requires voters to weigh multiple aspects of a person’s record, character or values.
“They just have the policy question, and voters sort it out for themselves,” Stutzman said.
Those centrist tendencies helped push Prop. 42, one of two measures put on the ballot by billionaires trying to protect their wealth, across the finish line. That measure bans taxes on personal property, business interests and financial investments. The Associated Press confirmed its passage by 51.3% Friday.
Anti-tax and union supporters touted it as a way to protect retirement savings and pensions potentially targeted by the billionaire tax, though billionaire tax proponents countered that their measure never targeted ordinary retirement accounts in the first place.
Experts say voter confusion and a $378 million opposition warchest donated primarily by Silicon Valley tech billionaires doomed the billionaire tax.
Props. 41 and 42 were designed specifically to kill Prop. 40 if it had passed, creating a chaotic array of choices. The billionaire tax also amassed a coalition of diverse and vocal opponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, Planned Parenthood, medical clinics and the state’s largest teachers union, despite the California Democratic Party and California Labor Federation supporting it.
Polling showed support for the measure dropped 6 points in the last two months before the election, taking it from a narrow lead to a crushing defeat. 
“The campaign against the billionaire tax was a success,” Grose said.
Other taxes succeeded
But few view the results on Prop. 40 as a referendum on the state’s progressive tax system. Instead, many analysts said it was simply bad policy that splintered California’s Democratic base.
Prop. 40 aimed to focus almost all the revenue in healthcare while cutting out other areas of state spending, which would lose funding if billionaires left the state and stopped paying income taxes, said Thad Kousser, a political science professor at UC San Diego. That, he said, was “an unforced error.” 
“It made it a David and Goliath fight, but it didn’t need to be,” he said. “You don’t pass a landmark progressive tax increase that is sort of a change to how America has historically done anything by dividing up the progressive coalition.”
At the same time, Prop. 42’s anti-taxation sentiment was also somewhat tempered by the defeat of Prop. 43, which would have made increasing taxes for local public services more difficult, and the success of Prop. 3, which sticks a higher tax bracket on high-income earners to help fund schools.
Prop. 43 would have required a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax dedicated to specific services. Kousser said voters are concerned the measure would allow for “minority rule,” where just a third of voters would be able to block essential funding for local services.
“Voters don’t like to put in place these rules that seem to be tilted in one direction,” he said.
David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, said Prop. 3’s passage sent a “resounding message of support for taxing the wealthy.” That measure passed with nearly 59% of the vote and sets a higher tax bracket on individually earned income above $360,000.
People in that income bracket have been paying that extra tax since 2012 as a temporary state budget fix; Prop. 3 made it permanent.
Why could voters distinguish between the income tax Prop. 3 and the wealth tax in Prop. 40? Partly because Prop. 3 had no opposition among Democrats, Kousser noted. It also extended an existing tax, whereas Prop. 40 opponents ran ads claiming that state lawmakers could come after average Californians’ personal savings.
Ballot box tempting for revenue seekers
Dustin Corcoran, chief executive of the California Medical Association, which opposed the billionaire tax, said he also does not view its defeat “as an endorsement of wealth inequality or the status quo.”
The state still needs to find a way to securely finance healthcare, education and other core services, Corcoran said, and the medical association is exploring future ballot initiative options to generate revenue. 
Not even Prop. 40’s supporters view its defeat as a reason to stop trying to tax the ultra-wealthy in California. Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponents of the billionaire tax, vowed to come back in 2028 with another billionaire tax initiative.
Regan also pushed back on the notion that Democrats were divided on wealth taxes, arguing that polling showed between 60% to 70% of Democrats supported the measure and only Democratic leaders such as Newsom and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra opposed it. 
“At the very highest levels of state officials there’s actually, you know, a different point of view, but that’s out of step with where regular people are at,” Regan said. 
Still, fiscal conservatives, the state’s non-partisan budget analyst, and even some moderate Democrats say taxation cannot be the only solution to California’s budget woes. The state has faced four consecutive deficit years and spending that outpaces revenue despite the budget as a whole growing. The current state budget calls for $351.7 billion in total spending — a 64% increase over the $214.8 billion Newsom signed in his first year as governor seven years ago.
“California’s budget is structurally overextended despite booming and near-record revenues,” the Legislative Analyst’s Office wrote in a new budget assessment. “This overextended budget reflects a higher ongoing spending base; diminished reserves; an already accumulated wall of debt; and annual, out-year operating deficits of $8 billion to $10 billion.”

text:
Scaffolding on the State Capitol of Wisconsin | Photo by Greg AndersonThere are a lot of big things Democrats in Wisconsin can do with their new, trifecta control of state government. Reinvesting in public schools — and shifting the burden for keeping schools afloat off local property taxpayers — would be a great start. So would overturning Act 10 (unless the state Supreme Court beats them to it), restoring the prevailing wage law and getting rid of so-called right-to-work legislation, thus reversing the largest decline in union representation in any state over the last 40 years. Add to that getting rid of PFAS, preserving public land, creating a nonpartisan redistricting process that ends gerrymandering once and for all. All of these things are possible when the new governor and Legislature get to work. 
While state officials can’t reverse federal policies that are driving up the cost of living, let alone end the disastrous Iran war, they can do a lot to improve the material wellbeing of state residents just by turning the page on 15 years of austerity.
Wisconsin is sitting on a state budget surplus that mostly represents the money the state no longer pays to support schools. For more than a decade, Wisconsin has let its education historic system degrade while hoarding that money. 
At the same time, local property taxpayers are overextended and grouchy from years of reaching into their own pockets to make up for the state’s failure to support schools.
Former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker’s assault on unions hurt teachers and other public employees directly, but it also created a much harsher, leaner environment for working people across Wisconsin and their families. 
A recent report by the Illinois Economic Policy Institute highlights the ways anti-union policies in Wisconsin have harmed the middle class, degraded a once-great public school system and made life more expensive and less secure for working families. 
This was not what Walker and his allies advertised when they pioneered the divide-and-conquer politics that pushed down union membership, wages and labor force participation for both union and non-union workers. 
Supposedly, busting teachers’ unions was going to give schools the budget flexibility to do more with less, and slashing state funding for education would mean lower taxes. Instead, schools went into a long financial slide, accompanied by cuts to programs, increasing class sizes and declining test scores, while property tax rates soared. 
Walker and the Republicans talked a lot about making Wisconsin “open for business” and ushering in a new era of prosperity. But the promised 250,000 new private sector jobs never materialized, and wages, job growth and GDP languished compared to our neighboring Great Lakes states, as “data wonk” Bruce Thompson wrote in an analysis for Urban Milwaukee of the effects of Act 10.
All of this, plus Republicans’ stubborn refusal to accept the federal Medicaid expansion for years before President Donald Trump’s massive assault on healthcare, contributed to Wisconsinites’ particular struggles with affordability — the issue that drove the blue tsunami across the country in the 2026 midterms.
Voters in the last election expressed serious doubt about some of the core tenets of Republican economic policy, including the idea that tax breaks for the very rich will make us all more prosperous, and spending on schools and other basic social goods is a burdensome waste. 
In the Republican radio address this week, incoming Republican Senate minority leader Julian Bradley acknowledged the stunning midterm rebuke to his party, saying “folks who are struggling to get by want to know that there’s a path to get ahead.”
“We hear you,” he said on behalf of his fellow members of Wisconsin’s severely diminished Republican caucus. Then he doubled down on the philosophy that got them where they are today: “If the new Democrat majority wants to focus on affordability, then we should be talking about meaningful tax cuts, returning the surplus to the families who earned it and clearing away the red tape that makes it harder to build a home or hire a worker.”
If voters wanted more of the same Republican tax cuts and deregulation Bradley is pushing, and which reached a new peak with Trump’s massive “One Big Beautiful” transfer of wealth from the many to the few, the election wouldn’t have gone the way it did.
According to Bradley, Democrats are talking about “higher taxes, more spending, redrawing maps” and “not a single one of these ideas will lower your grocery bills.”
It’s true that ending Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran that is driving record-high diesel prices would be the fastest route to cheaper groceries. But state Democrats can do a lot to improve Wisconsinites’ economic wellbeing by bringing back middle class jobs and union protections that raise wages. Using state money to support schools will lower property taxes. Investing in healthcare, child care, mass transit, environmental protection and clean energy will improve the economy and the future of our state.
Wisconsinites are eager to see government get to work to get those things done.
